chapters.name: Chapter 1: Thinking like a security analyst

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The analyst job and the Security+ exam
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose the right Security+ exam version for your test date and list its domains.
This lesson builds toward: Using the official CompTIA Security+ pages, you will write a study and test plan that names the exam version and a target date, covering every domain with its weight and weekly study time.
Entry security jobs include security analyst, SOC analyst (security operations center), and security or systems administrator. Analysts watch alerts and logs, check that systems are set up safely, and help respond to incidents. Many start in IT support and move up.
CompTIA Security+ is granted by CompTIA when you pass one exam. When we checked in October 2026, the exam had up to 90 questions in 90 minutes, multiple-choice and performance-based. CompTIA recommends Network+ and about two years of security or systems admin experience, but it lists these as recommended experience.
The exam is changing. Version 7 (SY0-701) is available now; its English exam was set to retire on 11 June 2027. Version 8 (SY0-801) was expected on or around 17 November 2026. If your test date is well into 2027, study for V8. If you will test soon, V7 may fit. Check the official pages: dates can move.
Each version lists five domains with weights. In both, security operations is the largest (about 27 to 28 percent). Your study time should follow the weights.
Step by step:
- Open the official Security+ page and the V7 and V8 exam pages.
- Pick your target test date.
- Choose the version that will be available on that date.
- Write down its exam code, five domains and weights.
- Check the current price and testing options on the official site.
Words to know:
- SOC: security operations center: the team that watches an organization's systems for attacks.
- Security analyst: a person who watches for, checks and responds to security problems.
- Exam version: a version of the exam with its own code and topics; old versions retire.
- Retire: when an exam version stops being offered.
Official sources:
- CompTIA Security+ certification (official page)
- CompTIA Security+ V7 (SY0-701) exam details
- CompTIA Security+ V8 (SY0-801) exam details
Try it now: Choose a target test month. Using the official pages, decide V7 or V8 and write one sentence saying why. Then list that version's five domains with their weights and circle the largest.
You can now say what an entry security analyst does, choose the right Security+ version for your test date, and list its domains.

check.q: You plan to test in late 2027. Which version should you study for?
options: Any version; they are the same
V8 (SY0-801), because V7 English is set to retire in June 2027
check.why: Study for the version that will still be offered on your test date; check the official pages.

options: CompTIA, when you pass the exam
check.why: CompTIA grants Security+; this course prepares you for the exam.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The CIA triad, threats, vulnerabilities and risk
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Classify a security problem with the CIA triad and rate its risk.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short security scenario, you will classify which part of the CIA triad (confidentiality, integrity or availability) it harms, getting at least 4 of 5 right. Given a threat to an organization, you will rate its risk by likelihood and impact and choose a control type to reduce it, with a reason for the rating and the control.
Security protects three things, called the CIA triad. Confidentiality: only the right people can see data. Integrity: data is correct and not changed without permission. Availability: systems and data work when people need them.
Examples: a stolen laptop with customer files harms confidentiality. Someone changing payroll numbers harms integrity. Ransomware that locks every file, or a website knocked offline, harms availability.
A threat is something that could cause harm (a thief, a scammer, a storm). A vulnerability is a weakness it could use (an unpatched computer, a weak password, an unlocked door). Risk is how likely the harm is, times how bad it would be (the impact).
Analysts often rate risk on a simple grid: likelihood low, medium or high, and impact low, medium or high. High likelihood and high impact go to the top of the list.
Step by step:
- Name what could be harmed.
- Ask: does it hurt confidentiality, integrity or availability?
- Name the threat and the vulnerability.
- Rate likelihood: low, medium or high.
- Rate impact: low, medium or high.
- Put the high-high risks first.
Words to know:
- CIA triad: confidentiality, integrity and availability: the three goals of security.
- Threat: something or someone that could cause harm.
- Vulnerability: a weakness that a threat could use.
- Risk: how likely a harm is and how bad it would be.
- Ransomware: malware that locks files and demands payment.
Try it now: For a small business you know (a corner store, a church office, a clinic front desk), list three things that could go wrong. For each, write which CIA part it harms, the threat, the vulnerability, and a likelihood and impact rating.
You can now sort a security problem by the CIA triad and rate its risk by likelihood and impact.

check.q: Someone changes the amounts on invoices without permission. Which part of the CIA triad is harmed?
check.why: Integrity means data stays correct; unauthorized changes break it.

check.q: An office computer has not been updated in a year. In risk terms, the missing updates are a:
check.why: A missing update is a weakness that a threat could use.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Security controls and least privilege
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose a control type to reduce a given risk.
This lesson builds toward: Given a threat to an organization, you will rate its risk by likelihood and impact and choose a control type to reduce it, with a reason for the rating and the control.
A control is anything that reduces risk. Security+ sorts controls in two ways. By category: technical (a firewall, encryption, multifactor authentication), managerial (policies, risk assessments), operational (training, guards, procedures people follow) and physical (locks, badges, cameras).
By what they do: preventive controls stop an attack (a lock, multifactor authentication). Detective controls notice it (a camera, log alerts). Corrective controls fix things after (restoring from a backup). Deterrent controls discourage it (a warning sign). Compensating controls stand in when the main control is not possible.
A key rule is least privilege: give each person only the access they need for their job, and no more. A cashier does not need access to payroll. If an account is taken over, least privilege limits the damage.
Good defense uses several layers, so if one fails, another still protects (defense in depth).
Words to know:
- Control: anything that reduces a risk.
- Preventive / detective / corrective: controls that stop, notice, or fix a security problem.
- Least privilege: giving each person only the access their job needs.
- Defense in depth: using several layers of protection.
- Firewall: a tool that allows or blocks network traffic based on rules.
Official sources:
- CompTIA Security+ V7 (SY0-701) exam details
- CompTIA Security+ V8 (SY0-801) exam details
Try it now: Take the three risks from Lesson 2. For each, choose one control. Write its category (technical, managerial, operational or physical) and what it does (preventive, detective or corrective). Then write one least-privilege rule for that business.
You can now pick a control for a risk, name its category and type, and apply least privilege.

check.q: A security camera that records who enters is mainly which type of control?
check.why: Cameras notice and record events, which makes them detective (and physical) controls.

check.q: A new cashier asks for access to the payroll system. Using least privilege, you:
options: Give full admin access to be safe
Give access only if the job truly needs it
check.why: Least privilege grants only the access a role needs.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Hardening your own computer
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check and record the main security settings on your own computer.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own Windows or Mac computer, you will check and record the update, firewall, antivirus, account type, screen lock and disk encryption settings, with every item checked and any gap written down.
Hardening means making a system harder to attack by turning on protections and turning off what is not needed. Analysts check this on company computers every day. Practice on your own computer only.
Check six things. Updates: are they installed? Firewall: is it on? Antivirus: is it on and current (Microsoft Defender is built into Windows; Macs have built-in malware protection)? Account type: do you use a standard account for daily work, with admin only when needed? Screen lock: does it lock after a few minutes and need a password or PIN? Disk encryption: is it on (BitLocker or Device Encryption on many Windows computers, FileVault on Mac)?
On Windows, look in Settings for Windows Update and Accounts, and open Windows Security for the firewall and virus protection. On a Mac, look in System Settings for Software Update, Network > Firewall, Users & Groups, Lock Screen, and Privacy & Security > FileVault. Menu names can change between versions; search Settings if you cannot find one.
If you turn on disk encryption, save the recovery key somewhere safe and offline first. Without it you can lose your files. If you are not sure, write it down as a gap and ask for help instead.
Step by step:
- Updates: check and install.
- Firewall: confirm it is on.
- Antivirus: confirm it is on and current.
- Account: note whether your daily account is standard or admin.
- Screen lock: set it to lock after a few minutes.
- Disk encryption: check if it is on; save the recovery key before turning it on.
- Write each result and any gap.
Words to know:
- Hardening: making a system harder to attack by turning on protections and removing what is not needed.
- Disk encryption: scrambling everything on a drive so a thief cannot read it without the key.
- Recovery key: a long code that unlocks an encrypted drive if you cannot sign in.
- Baseline: the standard secure settings every computer in an organization should have.
Official sources:
- CISA: Cybersecurity best practices
Try it now: On your own computer, check all six items. Make a table with three columns: setting, what you found, and what to fix. This is part 1 of your final task.
You can now check a computer's main security settings and write down the gaps, the way an analyst checks a baseline.

check.q: Before turning on disk encryption, what should you do?
options: Save the recovery key somewhere safe and offline
check.why: Without the recovery key you could lose access to your own files.

check.q: Which account should you use for daily work?
options: A shared account with no password
A guest account with your files
check.why: A standard account limits what malware or mistakes can change.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Reading logs and spotting suspicious activity
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Flag the suspicious entries in a sign-in log and say why.
This lesson builds toward: Given a short sign-in log, you will flag the suspicious entries and explain why each is suspicious, finding every repeated failed sign-in and the odd success after them.
A log is a list of events a system records, each with a time. Analysts read sign-in logs to spot attacks. On Windows, Event Viewer keeps a Security log (viewing it needs an admin account); failed sign-ins appear as event 4625 and successful ones as 4624. Here we use a made-up log instead.
Practice log (made up): 02:14:01 FAILED user=jlopez from 203.0.113.50. 02:14:03 FAILED user=jlopez from 203.0.113.50. 02:14:05 FAILED user=jlopez from 203.0.113.50. 02:14:07 FAILED user=jlopez from 203.0.113.50. 02:14:09 SUCCESS user=jlopez from 203.0.113.50. 08:02:30 SUCCESS user=mchen from 10.0.0.12.
Warning signs: many failed sign-ins in a few seconds (someone guessing passwords), then a success from the same address (they may have guessed right). Also odd times (2 am for a 9-to-5 worker), sign-ins from an unusual place, and one account signing in from two far-apart places close together.
Your job is to notice, record and report, not to strike back. Write what you saw, the times, the account and the address, and pass it on following your team's process.
Step by step:
- Read each line: time, result, account, address.
- Look for many failures in a short time.
- Look for a success right after failures from the same address.
- Look for odd times or places.
- Write down each suspicious line and why.
- Report it; never try to get into the other system yourself.
Words to know:
- Log: a time-stamped list of events a system records.
- Event Viewer: the Windows tool for reading system and security logs.
- Brute force: guessing a password by trying many options very fast.
- Indicator: a clue in data that something bad may be happening.
Try it now: Copy the practice log onto paper. Circle each suspicious line and write why. Rate the risk (likelihood and impact) and the CIA part at risk. Keep this for part 2 of your final task.
You can now read a sign-in log, flag the suspicious entries, and explain why they matter.

check.q: In the practice log, which line is the most worrying?
options: The 02:14:09 success for jlopez right after four failures
None; failed sign-ins are always normal
check.why: A success right after rapid failures from the same address suggests a password was guessed.

check.q: You find signs of an attack in a log. What do you do?
options: Record the details and report them through your team's process
check.why: Analysts record and report; striking back is illegal and deleting logs destroys evidence.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Incident response, and your Security+ plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: List the incident response steps for a scenario and write a dated Security+ study plan.
This lesson builds toward: Given a security incident scenario, you will list the incident response steps in order and write one action for each, with no step missing and evidence kept. Using the official CompTIA Security+ pages, you will write a study and test plan that names the exam version and a target date, covering every domain with its weight and weekly study time.
An incident is a security event that causes or threatens harm. Organizations follow set steps so people stay calm. Security+ uses: preparation, detection, analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, and lessons learned.
For the jlopez sign-in: preparation (the team already has a plan and contacts); detection (you spot the log entries); analysis (confirm it is real: did jlopez sign in at 2 am?); containment (lock the account and end its sessions); eradication (reset the password, turn on multifactor authentication, remove anything the attacker set up); recovery (give jlopez safe access back and watch the account); lessons learned (what would have stopped this?).
Keep evidence: do not delete logs or wipe a computer before your team says so. Write times and actions as you go. Report to the person your process names.
Now plan your exam. Use the version you chose in Lesson 1. Set a target date. Give more weeks to the bigger domains. Practice with the official exam objectives, your own hardening and log notes, and the checks here. Choose weekly hours that fit your life. Before booking, check the price and testing options on the official page, and ask workforce, veterans or reentry programs about help with costs.
Step by step:
- Preparation: know the plan and who to call.
- Detection: notice the warning signs.
- Analysis: confirm it is real and how bad.
- Containment: stop it spreading.
- Eradication: remove the cause.
- Recovery: return to normal and watch.
- Lessons learned: write what to change.
- Plan: version, target date, domains and weights, weekly hours.
Words to know:
- Incident: a security event that causes or threatens harm.
- Containment: stopping an incident from spreading.
- Eradication: removing the cause of an incident.
- Evidence: logs, files and notes that show what happened; they must be kept.
Official sources:
- CompTIA Security+ certification (official page)
- CompTIA Security+ V7 (SY0-701) exam details
- CompTIA Security+ V8 (SY0-801) exam details
Try it now: Final task: put together your hardening table (Lesson 4), an incident note for the jlopez log with its CIA impact, risk rating and one action for each response step, and your Security+ plan with version, target date, domains and weights, and weekly hours.
You can now follow the incident response steps for a real-looking case and follow your own dated plan toward Security+.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Hardening table Some of the six settings are not checked. All six settings checked on your own computer, with results and gaps. Each gap has a fix and a reason, and the recovery key plan is written down. Log review Misses the rapid failures or the success after them. Flags every suspicious line and says why. Also names what normal looks like and what extra data would confirm it. CIA and risk No CIA part named, or the wrong one. Names the CIA part at risk and gives a likelihood and impact rating with a reason. Explains how the risk could change if a control were added. Controls No control, or a control that does not fit the risk. Names at least one fitting control with its category and type. Uses layered controls and a least-privilege rule. Incident steps Steps missing or out of order, or evidence destroyed. All seven steps in order, each with one action, and evidence kept. Names who is told at each step and how lessons learned would change the setup. Study and test plan No version or date, or domains missing. Names V7 or V8 with a reason, a target date, every domain with its weight and weekly hours. Gives more weeks to heavier domains and names where to check price and get help with costs. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: You confirm an account was taken over. What is the next step?
options: Containment: lock the account and end its sessions
check.why: After detection and analysis, you contain the incident so it cannot spread.

check.q: Which belongs in a Security+ study plan?
options: A list of hacking tools to try on others
The exam version, a target date, domains with weights and weekly hours
check.why: A plan names the right version, a date, what to study and when.
